chapter.title: Three Copies
chapter.sub: The off-site copy stopped nineteen days ago and said nothing. The backup was a mirror.

items.text: SEASON 10 · EPISODE 9 · DRAFT  Coldframe Sound · week six · Maya, Pim and Hollis · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Three weeks from the end of the album, Pim notices a date on the backup screen. It’s nineteen days old. By Monday night the word “backup” has stopped meaning what anyone thought.  ⚑ RV-176: the files are the artists’ work in the studio’s care. RV-177: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: Three Copies
items.stakes: The off-site backup stopped nineteen days ago and said nothing. The ‘backup’ in the machine room is a mirror.
items.reward: The album in two buildings tonight — and a backup that's been restored, not just ticked.

objectives.text: Decide how you'll know it works

items.rumor: A backup is a restore you've already done.

hints.text: What exists nowhere but here — and how fast can it be somewhere else?

options.label: Buy more cloud storage and restart the upload
options.result: It restarts — at 72 GB a night against 166 GB a day. It will never catch up.
options.consequence: Fixes the stop and not the arithmetic.

options.label: Measure what exists only in this building; copy it tonight to a new drive that Hollis takes home
options.result: About 2.3 TB. Four and a quarter hours at 150 MB/s. Hollis drives it home at eleven.
options.consequence: Size the risk, then get one copy into another building tonight.

options.label: Relax — there's the mirror in the machine room
options.result: The mirror is in the same building, and it copies mistakes.
options.consequence: Trusts a word, not a test.

options.label: Stop recording until the backups catch up
options.result: Esme loses three days she doesn't have.
options.consequence: Safe, and it costs the artist instead of fixing the system.

items.title: Nineteen days behind.
items.body: The cloud account filled nineteen days ago and paused, emailing a mailbox nobody reads. But the arithmetic was broken long before: a tracking day writes about 166 GB, and 20 Mb/s for eight hours a night moves 72 GB. Even running, the upload fell 94 GB further behind every tracking day.
items.label: Test: how far behind — and could it ever have kept up?

items.title: ‘storage full — uploads paused’
items.body: An automated email, nineteen days old, in an inbox nobody reads: ‘Your storage is full. Uploads have been paused.’ Sent to backups@ — a mailbox that forwards to a technician who left in 2021.

items.title: Beyond the reach of accident
items.body: In 1791 Thomas Jefferson, worried that the new nation's founding papers were rotting in public offices, wrote that the way to save them was not by locking the originals away — ‘not by vaults and locks… but by such a multiplication of copies, as shall place them beyond the reach of accident.’ Archivists still quote him. So, now, does Pim.

items.text: Act II — “A mirror isn't a backup”

items.title: A mirror isn't a backup.
items.body: While the gap copies, Pim goes pale. That morning he deleted a folder he thought was old takes — Esme's alternate ballad vocals, the only copy. He'd meant to restore it ‘from the backup’. The mirror deleted it on both drives the instant he did; the off-site copy predates the session. The files come back from the recording computer's own trash, which nobody had emptied. Luck.
items.label: Test: how long would a cloud restore take — and what actually saved the vocals?

items.alt: The control room at night; Pim, hands out, stricken; Hollis quiet beside the console.

bubbles.text: I thought the mirror was the backup. Everyone said it was.
I said it. I wrote ‘BACKUP’ on the box.

items.prompt: I thought the mirror was the backup. Everyone said it was.

options.label: “Everyone was trusting a word. Today you tested it — with a real mistake. That's worth more than the files.”
options.reply: Can I own the restore tests? Like — mine?

options.label: “It's fine, we got lucky.”
options.reply: That's the bit that scares me.

hints.text: Which copy survives a fire, and which survives a mistake?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S10E09). Option B needs Redundancy at LIMITED or better — independent copies.

options.label: A bigger mirror
options.result: More space for the same mistakes.
options.consequence: Still copies every deletion, in the same room.

options.label: 3-2-1: the session drive; an hourly versioned backup to a separate device that keeps deletions for 30 days; off-site, two drives rotated weekly — Hollis takes one home every Friday — plus a nightly cloud copy of the day's new work; an alert when the backlog passes a day
options.result: Hollis signs for the drives and the versioned device. Pim owns the Friday swap. The first alert test fires on cue.
options.consequence: Copies that survive a fire and a mistake, and a system that shouts when it falls behind.

options.label: An hourly versioned backup only; off-site ‘when Hollis remembers’
options.result: Mistakes are covered. The fire isn't, most weeks.
options.consequence: The best you can do without independent copies — and it's still one building.

options.label: Cloud only, on a faster connection
options.result: It keeps up — and a full restore still takes days.
options.consequence: Off-site, but slow to bring back and no local versions.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #100 · AVERY'S LENS  A backup is a restore you've already done  Three copies, two kinds of storage, one somewhere else — kept in versions, watched for backlog, and restored on a schedule. A green tick isn't evidence; a restored, playing session is.  The off-site copy said ‘up to date’ for nineteen days after it stopped, and the ‘backup’ deleted the only copy of a vocal the moment Pim did.

items.alt: The backup sheet after the change: on the right, four green units — the session drive, an hourly versioned backup keeping 30 days, off-site drives A and B rotated on Fridays, and the cloud carrying each day's new work; a restore test of 4 TB at 150 MB/s, about 7.4 hours, done and repeated monthly.
items.caption: Three copies, two kinds, one elsewhere.

items.title: ‘BACKUP (RAID)’
items.body: A label on the machine-room enclosure in Hollis's handwriting: ‘BACKUP (RAID)’. He'd written it the day it arrived. It had been a mirror the whole time.

items.prompt: Everything is in place. How will you know it works?
items.risk: Finding out on the worst day.

hints.text: What would you have to do to be sure you could get the album back?

options.label: Trust the green ticks
options.result: Green ticks said ‘up to date’ for nineteen days.
options.consequence: A tick says a job finished, not that you can get your files back.

options.label: A restore test now — a whole session from the off-site drive to a different computer, opened, played and timed — then monthly, on the calendar, owned by Pim
options.result: Seven hours twenty-four minutes for four terabytes. Everyone now knows how long ‘restore’ means.
options.consequence: The only proof of a backup is a restore.

options.label: Check that the file counts match on every copy
options.result: They match. It says nothing about whether the files open.

options.label: Ask the backup software's vendor to certify it

items.label: **Service Mode:** run the Monday night yourself.

items.alt: Outside Coldframe Sound on Friday evening; Hollis holds a boxed drive under his arm; Pim waves him off.

bubbles.text: Drive B. It lives in my kitchen now, next to the bread bin.
And next Friday you bring it back and take A. I've set a reminder. And an alert.

Then we have a decision before we have a take.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Three copies, two kinds of storage, one somewhere else. A mirror copies mistakes; versions keep what was there before. Do the arithmetic before you trust an upload (S = r × t, with bits and bytes kept straight) and before you promise a restore (t = S ÷ r). Alert on backlog, not just failure. A backup is a restore you have already done: whole, on another computer, opened, played and timed — on a calendar, with an owner.
